chunks: Branch prediction and its algorithms. The question: What is branch prediction? Describe some branch prediction algorithms.
A branch is an instruction that may jump somewhere else instead of continuing.

A modern CPU works on several instructions at once, like an assembly line (a pipeline), so it must keep fetching new ones before the branch's outcome is known, so the CPU makes a guess based on past behavior.
A right guess costs nothing. A wrong guess throws away the work done on the wrong path.
Imagine a driver who has turned left at the same fork every morning. Today the driver keeps going left without checking the map. Usually that saves time.
On the rare day the road goes right, the driver must turn around and loses time. A predictor works like that driver, learning from history.
At the same 5% miss rate a 2-cycle penalty costs 2% in CPI, while a 15-cycle penalty costs 15% and a 25-cycle penalty 25%.
Deeper pipelines make accuracy far more valuable, which is why predictors got so elaborate.
Taken / not taken: a branch is taken when it jumps and not taken when execution continues to the next instruction.
Misprediction penalty: cycles lost when the guess is wrong, roughly how many stages deep the branch is resolved ("The five-stage pipeline").
History: a record of how a branch behaved before, kept in a small table. 2-bit counter: a counter from 0 to 3 that predicts "taken" when 2 or 3.
It takes two wrong outcomes in a row to change the prediction.
A loop runs 10 times. Its branch at the end is taken 9 times, then not taken once, and then the loop starts again.
A predictor that just repeats the last outcome is wrong at the exit and wrong again at the next visit's first pass. That is 2 misses in 10, or 80% accurate.
A 2-bit counter stays on "taken" after the single not-taken exit, so it misses only once. That is 90% accurate.
That is the whole idea: guess from history, and a bit of memory beats none.
"Branch prediction is the CPU guessing a branch's direction and target before it resolves, so a pipeline can keep fetching instead of stalling.
A wrong guess flushes the speculative instructions and costs the pipeline depth in cycles. Static schemes are always-not-taken or backward-taken.
The standard dynamic one is a table of 2-bit saturating counters indexed by the PC, which mispredicts a loop only once at the exit instead of twice like a 1-bit predictor.
Better ones like gshare also use global branch history, and a BTB supplies the target address."
